pages.title: Soil Composition Basics
pages.subtitle: Balancing sand, silt, and clay for mechanical stabilization
pages.content: Interlocking blocks rely on optimal soil particle distribution rather than high cement content. Clay acts as a natural binder, while sand provides the structural skeleton. Ideal ICSEB soil contains 50–70% sand, 15–30% silt, and 10–20% clay. Too much clay causes swelling and severe shrinkage cracking upon drying; too little clay results in a crumbly block that lacks green strength before curing.
pages.imagePrompt: Technical vector diagram illustrating soil grain size distribution for ICSEB production. Shows a settling jar test with distinct layers of sand at the bottom, silt in the middle, clay on top.

actionCallout.label: TRY THIS TODAY
actionCallout.content: Perform a simple Jar Test: fill a straight-sided glass jar 1/3 full with dry field soil, add water and 1 tsp salt, shake vigorously for 2 minutes.

pages.title: Hydration Mechanics
pages.subtitle: How OPC cement bonds soil particles under compaction
pages.content: Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) stabilizes soil through chemical hydration, creating calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gels that lock soil grains together. Soil moisture during compaction must equal the Optimum Moisture Content (OMC)—typically 8–12% by weight. If the soil is too dry, cement hydration fails and air pockets remain.
pages.imagePrompt: Resilience diagram showing chemical hydration of cement bonding soil particles under compaction, with fallback drop for dry mix.

actionCallout.label: DO THIS TODAY
actionCallout.content: Perform the Drop Test: squeeze a handful of moist soil-cement mix into a ball, drop it from 1 meter height onto hard ground.

pages.title: Curing Chemistry
pages.subtitle: Managing moisture retention for full strength gain
pages.content: ICSEB blocks do not harden by drying out; they harden through moisture-dependent chemical reaction. Premature drying stops cement hydration, causing up to 60% loss in ultimate compressive strength. Blocks must maintain near 100% relative humidity for at least 7 days to reach initial structural integrity, and 28 days for full strength.
pages.imagePrompt: Process diagram illustrating hydration reaction and moisture retention over 28-day curing cycle.

actionCallout.label: BUILD THIS ONCE
actionCallout.content: Set up a dedicated curing pad using thick 200-micron black polythene sheeting on a flat shaded surface, elevated on wooden pallets.
